I'm writing a data-driven story for ConsumerAffairs ranking the 100 largest U.S. metros by how much property taxes have risen relative to home values in the last few years. Looking for these qualified US-based experts who can provide insightful written responses to a few questions (more detailed answers to a couple will be more helpful than surface-level ones to all): - Property tax/public finance experts - Housing economists/real estate economists - Urban economics/local government finance academics - Property tax policy researchers - Assessors or assessment professionals 1. Why do property taxes rise? Can you explain how property taxes work and why they can vary so much from one place to another? 2. What can homeowners do about rising property taxes? Please share 3-5 actionable tips and briefly explain each. 3. Sometimes a metro's home values fall slightly, and property taxes fall even more sharply the same year. What usually explains taxes moving faster than values in a case like that? 4. Property tax growth can look very different for homeowners with a mortgage vs. one without in the same metro. What usually drives that gap? 5. It's rare, but occasionally a metro sees property tax bills fall over a two-year period even as home values rise. What would typically cause that? 6. A metro can have one of the highest dollar property tax bills in the country while its effective tax rate (tax as a % of home value) is flat or falling. How should homeowners think about that difference? 7. When people look at their tax bill, is nominal dollar growth misleading compared to what's happened after inflation? How big a difference does that usually make? Finally, please provide: 1) source's role/title, LinkedIn profile, company website, and company descriptor 2) source's email IMPORTANT: NO AI responses, or responses you've already submitted elsewhere. Given the volume of source requests I send out, I can't respond to check-ins. Rest assured that if your response is a strong fit, I'll use it. I also don't have visibility into publish dates once a piece is with editorial, so I can't provide those either. Thanks so much for understanding! _____

If this appeals to you, please closely read the brief, important points below before proceeding to the interview questions and precisely following the instructions. --------------------------------------- 1. Briefly introduce yourself. 2. Please, no use of AI. I value your brain, not answers from technology. Please don't use AI in any form in your reply. 3. Copy and paste the questions (and question numbers) into your reply. Create a new paragraph, with a double space between the question and your answer. This is easier on my eyes and brain. 4. No backlinks offered yet your name, brief professional title, expertise and business are highlighted and added to article tags for SEO and AI finding purposes. 5. Please send a professional headshot, perfectly focused and medium large to accompany the article, to rep.intel.news@gmail.com ------------------------ INTERVIEW Copy and paste the questions (and question numbers into your reply and double space between each question and your answers). No AI in your responses. 1) Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei: "I won't lie to you—there are real dangers," Amodei told CBS. "And I think for too long the industry lied to people about the fact that this technology had risks." This can't be a throwaway line and seems like it should be discussed. Whether it was ignorance of as Amodei said, a lie, how does this affect the trust levels and benefit of the doubt between AI leaders and their companies with government, the media, investors and the general public? Are they worthy of forgiveness or amplified scrutiny? 2) "I don't think I fully just appreciated what it would actually be like when the progress was as fast as it was," he added, which seems to be a little more believable. How much should government, media and the public take that point into consideration when judging AI leaders and their judgment? 3) "It doesn't mean we need to panic today,” Amodei told CBS. “It doesn't mean we need to shut it all down. But I would say it's a warning sign. It's a warning sign that we need to slow down." Why was pace not a concern until now or at least as much of one as it should have been all along? What has been getting in the way and what errors were glaring? _____

I'm looking for an aviation, aerospace supply-chain, or China industrial-policy expert for a 30-45 minute recorded interview for my YouTube channel. The video is a documentary-style deep dive into the Comac C919, working angle: Why China Built The World's Most American Airliner. The C919 is China's answer to Boeing and Airbus. It took seventeen years and tens of billions of dollars, and it is meant to end China's dependence on Western aircraft. Yet the engines are CFM LEAP-1C from GE and Safran, and the avionics, flight controls, landing gear, APU and most major systems come from American and European suppliers. When US engine export approvals paused in 2025, the production line stalled. China built an airframe and bought almost everything else from the companies it is trying to replace. The video is not a "Boeing killer" story or a "copy that can't fly without Western permission" story. It's about why China accepted that dependence, what the C919 is actually for, and whether a fully Chinese version is realistic within a decade. I'd like someone who can explain: Why Comac chose Western suppliers rather than domestic ones, and whether it had a choice What the C919 actually is: how much is Chinese by value, and which systems matter most The CJ-1000A engine programme and how far it realistically is from certification How the 2025 export-licence pause affected production, and what it revealed about leverage What the C919 is really for: domestic market capture, industrial learning, bargaining power with Boeing and Airbus, or all three Why China's domestic airlines are ordering it, and on what terms Whether EASA or FAA certification is achievable, and whether it matters How this compares with Japan's failed SpaceJet and Russia's MC-21 What a "fully Chinese" C919 would take, and by when Whether Boeing and Airbus should be worried, and on what timescale Ideal sources: aerospace analysts, aircraft supply-chain specialists, engine industry experts, former Boeing, Airbus, GE, Safran or Comac-supplier staff, China industrial-policy academics, and journalists who have covered Comac closely. I'm looking for a transport, infrastructure, aviation or rail expert for a 30-45 minute recorded interview for my YouTube channel. The video is a documentary-style deep dive into why Australia never built high-speed rail, working angle: Why Australia's Busiest Route Has No Train. Sydney-Melbourne is one of the world's busiest air corridors, comparable to Tokyo-Osaka and Madrid-Barcelona, both transformed by high-speed rail decades ago. The east coast is denser than Spain. Governments have studied a line since the 1980s. Yet the first stage actually funded runs Newcastle to Sydney, a commuter corridor airlines don't serve, with a construction decision not due until 2028 and Sydney-Melbourne still decades away. The video is not for or against rail. It's about why the numbers that worked in Japan, Spain and Italy keep failing in Australia, what that has meant for Qantas and domestic aviation, and whether the Newcastle line is the start of something real or another study that goes nowhere. I'd like someone who can explain: Why every Australian HSR proposal since the 1980s has stalled How geography, city spacing and population distribution change the economics versus Europe and Japan Why the first funded stage is Newcastle-Sydney, not Sydney-Melbourne or Sydney-Canberra The real cost drivers (tunnelling, land, the Hawkesbury crossing) and why estimates keep climbing How the Sydney-Melbourne air market evolved without rail, and whether Qantas and Virgin benefited structurally The rail-versus-air tipping point, and where Sydney-Melbourne and Sydney-Canberra would sit What happened to airlines in Spain, Italy and Japan when HSR arrived on trunk routes Whether airlines ever lobbied against rail, or that's a myth What the 2028 decision really means: hype versus funded, planned or under construction Ideal sources: rail and transport analysts, infrastructure economists, aviation analysts, transport planners, academics, former airline or rail executives, and anyone who worked on earlier Australian HSR studies. The interview takes 30-45 minutes over Zoom or similar, recorded and used in a long-form aviation/travel/business documentary with full name/title/company attribution. I'm after clear, accessible commentary that helps a broad international audience understand why Australia skipped high-speed rail, and whether that is finally about to change.

For MedCentral, I'm writing a deep dive on your recently published scientific statement by the Endocrine Society that obesity treatment outcomes should go beyond weight loss and focus on patient-centered, comprehensive health improvement. Here's the press release: https://www.endocrine.org/news-and-advocacy/news-room/2026/obesity-scientific-statement And the scientific statement: https://academic.oup.com/edrv/advance-article/doi/10.1210/endrev/bnag025/8786107 We aim to explore the need for this initiative, the top highlights from the scientific statement, and how it improves clinician knowledge, as well as areas of future research. My deadline is next week Wednesday EOD 09/23. Questions: 1. Importance of the statement: Why is this scientific statement important at this stage in the evolution of obesity treatment, particularly as newer medications are achieving substantially greater weight loss than earlier therapies? What gaps or challenges does it help address? 2.Clinical relevance: The statement emphasizes that treatment success may need to be assessed beyond percentage weight loss, including health outcomes, anthropometric measures, and body composition. Although the statement is not a clinical guideline, how might these concepts inform clinicians’ understanding of treatment response and the outcomes that matter most when caring for patients with obesity? 3.Changing understanding of obesity: The statement highlights the heterogeneity of obesity and treatment response, individualized treatment targets, body composition, and potentially weight-independent effects of obesity medications. How might these concepts change the way clinicians understand obesity and the goals of treatment going forward? 4.Future research: Which research priorities identified in the statement do you believe are most important for advancing obesity care over the next several years? Is there anything else in the scientific statement that you think clinicians and researchers should pay particular attention to? Any financial disclosures or biopharma affiliations?

I'm looking for an aviation, aerospace supply-chain, or China industrial-policy expert for a 30-45 minute recorded interview for my YouTube channel. The video is a documentary-style deep dive into the Comac C919, working angle: Why China Built The World's Most American Airliner. The C919 is China's answer to Boeing and Airbus. It took seventeen years and tens of billions of dollars, and it is meant to end China's dependence on Western aircraft. Yet the engines are CFM LEAP-1C from GE and Safran, and the avionics, flight controls, landing gear, APU and most major systems come from American and European suppliers. When US engine export approvals paused in 2025, the production line stalled. China built an airframe and bought almost everything else from the companies it is trying to replace. The video is not a "Boeing killer" story or a "copy that can't fly without Western permission" story. It's about why China accepted that dependence, what the C919 is actually for, and whether a fully Chinese version is realistic within a decade. I'd like someone who can explain: Why Comac chose Western suppliers rather than domestic ones, and whether it had a choice What the C919 actually is: how much is Chinese by value, and which systems matter most The CJ-1000A engine programme and how far it realistically is from certification How the 2025 export-licence pause affected production, and what it revealed about leverage What the C919 is really for: domestic market capture, industrial learning, bargaining power with Boeing and Airbus, or all three Why China's domestic airlines are ordering it, and on what terms Whether EASA or FAA certification is achievable, and whether it matters How this compares with Japan's failed SpaceJet and Russia's MC-21 What a "fully Chinese" C919 would take, and by when Whether Boeing and Airbus should be worried, and on what timescale Ideal sources: aerospace analysts, aircraft supply-chain specialists, engine industry experts, former Boeing, Airbus, GE, Safran or Comac-supplier staff, China industrial-policy academics, and journalists who have covered Comac closely. The interview takes 30-45 minutes over Zoom or similar, recorded and used in a long-form aviation/business documentary with full name/title/company attribution. I'm after clear, accessible commentary that helps a broad international audience understand why China built a plane it can't build alone, and what happens next.

I am writing an upcoming feature for Medscape exploring the intricate feedback loop between mental health and obesity, specifically zooming in on the interoceptive facet in this piece. For decades, many individuals struggling with obesity have been conditioned by diet culture, chronic stress, or trauma to override their internal biological cues. This feature examines how clinicians are utilizing somatic therapy and interoceptive awareness training to help patients safely reconnect with their bodies, teaching them how to accurately translate physical sensations like hunger, fatigue, and emotional triggers. I am looking to speak with board-certified psychiatrists, psychologists, behavioral obesity medicine specialists, and licensed somatic therapists who clinicalize these techniques. Questions: Please provide written responses (2-4 sentences per question) to the following five questions. Feel free to draw on clinical anecdotes (anonymized) or evidence-based practices. If you cite clinical studies in your answer, I'd really appreciate an accompanying link. From a clinical perspective, how do chronic stress, trauma, and decades of restrictive diet culture structurally alter a patient's ability to perceive and trust basic internal biological signals (e.g., true hunger, early satiety, and fatigue)? How do you define and introduce interoceptive awareness training to patients who are deeply disconnected from or distrustful of their physical sensations? What specific somatic therapy techniques or exercises have you found most effective in helping patients differentiate between genuine physiological hunger and emotional triggers (such as anxiety, boredom, or shame)? What are the biggest clinical hurdles or psychological safety barriers when patients begin to re-experience uncomfortable physical sensations, and how do you navigate them? How does restoring interoceptive awareness practically interrupt or mitigate the broader feedback loop between mental health distress and metabolic/weight challenges in long-term treatment? Submission Guidelines Format: Please answer the questions directly in your response or paste a secure link. Attachments will not be delivered to me via HARO. Credentials: Include your full name, full title as you'd like it published, and a headshot/bio link if available. Please also provide a disclosure statement relative to the issues covered.

I'm looking for a transport, infrastructure, aviation or rail expert for a 30-45 minute recorded interview for my YouTube channel. The video is a documentary-style deep dive into why Australia never built high-speed rail, working angle: Why Australia's Busiest Route Has No Train. Sydney-Melbourne is one of the world's busiest air corridors, comparable to Tokyo-Osaka and Madrid-Barcelona, both transformed by high-speed rail decades ago. The east coast is denser than Spain. Governments have studied a line since the 1980s. Yet the first stage actually funded runs Newcastle to Sydney, a commuter corridor airlines don't serve, with a construction decision not due until 2028 and Sydney-Melbourne still decades away. The video is not for or against rail. It's about why the numbers that worked in Japan, Spain and Italy keep failing in Australia, what that has meant for Qantas and domestic aviation, and whether the Newcastle line is the start of something real or another study that goes nowhere. I'd like someone who can explain: Why every Australian HSR proposal since the 1980s has stalled How geography, city spacing and population distribution change the economics versus Europe and Japan Why the first funded stage is Newcastle-Sydney, not Sydney-Melbourne or Sydney-Canberra The real cost drivers (tunnelling, land, the Hawkesbury crossing) and why estimates keep climbing How the Sydney-Melbourne air market evolved without rail, and whether Qantas and Virgin benefited structurally The rail-versus-air tipping point, and where Sydney-Melbourne and Sydney-Canberra would sit What happened to airlines in Spain, Italy and Japan when HSR arrived on trunk routes Whether airlines ever lobbied against rail, or that's a myth What the 2028 decision really means: hype versus funded, planned or under construction Ideal sources: rail and transport analysts, infrastructure economists, aviation analysts, transport planners, academics, former airline or rail executives, and anyone who worked on earlier Australian HSR studies. The interview takes 30-45 minutes over Zoom or similar, recorded and used in a long-form aviation/travel/business documentary with full name/title/company attribution. I'm after clear, accessible commentary that helps a broad international audience understand why Australia skipped high-speed rail, and whether that is finally about to change.

I'm looking for an aviation, aerospace supply-chain, or China industrial-policy expert for a 30-45 minute recorded interview for my YouTube channel. The video is a documentary-style deep dive into the Comac C919, working angle: Why China Built The World's Most American Airliner. The C919 is China's answer to Boeing and Airbus. It took seventeen years and tens of billions of dollars, and it is meant to end China's dependence on Western aircraft. Yet the engines are CFM LEAP-1C from GE and Safran, and the avionics, flight controls, landing gear, APU and most major systems come from American and European suppliers. When US engine export approvals paused in 2025, the production line stalled. China built an airframe and bought almost everything else from the companies it is trying to replace. The video is not a "Boeing killer" story or a "copy that can't fly without Western permission" story. It's about why China accepted that dependence, what the C919 is actually for, and whether a fully Chinese version is realistic within a decade. I'd like someone who can explain: Why Comac chose Western suppliers rather than domestic ones, and whether it had a choice What the C919 actually is: how much is Chinese by value, and which systems matter most The CJ-1000A engine programme and how far it realistically is from certification How the 2025 export-licence pause affected production, and what it revealed about leverage What the C919 is really for: domestic market capture, industrial learning, bargaining power with Boeing and Airbus, or all three Why China's domestic airlines are ordering it, and on what terms Whether EASA or FAA certification is achievable, and whether it matters How this compares with Japan's failed SpaceJet and Russia's MC-21 What a "fully Chinese" C919 would take, and by when Whether Boeing and Airbus should be worried, and on what timescale Ideal sources: aerospace analysts, aircraft supply-chain specialists, engine industry experts, former Boeing, Airbus, GE, Safran or Comac-supplier staff, China industrial-policy academics, and journalists who have covered Comac closely. The interview takes 30-45 minutes over Zoom or similar, recorded and used in a long-form aviation/business documentary with full name/title/company attribution. I'm after clear, accessible commentary that helps a broad international audience understand why China built a plane it can't build alone, and what happens next.

Reporting a feature for Deel Works. Most benefits and eligibility architecture was designed when 65 was a real exit date, and that assumption is still sitting inside plan documents. When someone doesn't leave, the rules produce consequences nobody planned for, usually one employee at a time, months after the cost lands. I need people who administer benefits inside a company. If you can't tell me your own eligibility hours threshold off the top of your head, you're not who I'm looking for. Not looking for: benefits brokers, consultants, PEO or benefits administration vendors, financial planners, retirement advisors, Medicare insurance agents, or anyone answering from the individual employee's planning side. PR representatives, please don't pitch clients whose companies sell benefits services. The hours threshold What is your benefits eligibility threshold in hours per week? When an employee reduced hours ahead of retirement, what happened to their coverage and retirement contributions? Did you carve out an exception, reclassify them, or let eligibility lapse? Have you ever declined an hours reduction because of what it would do to eligibility? What did you tell the employee? This is the one I most want to hear about. Who made that call — HR, finance, legal, the manager? Documented policy or one-off? Beyond health coverage, what else does someone lose when they drop below your threshold — retirement match, PTO accrual, life insurance, something else? Which causes the most trouble in practice? Job structure and pay Has your company changed a job description, title, or comp band to accommodate someone winding down? What was the constraint, and who had to approve it? Have you had someone stay in a role past the point where the job description still described what they did? What happened? HSA and Medicare Has an employee kept contributing to an HSA after becoming Medicare-eligible, or been caught by the six-month retroactive Part A rule? What happened, who noticed, and what did it cost them to unwind? Was it caught at enrollment, at payroll, or at tax filing? How far downstream matters to me. What do you send employees approaching 65, and at what age? If it's nothing beyond the summary plan description, please say so — that's a finding, not an embarrassment. Elder care Have you proposed an elder care benefit — referral, subsidy, backup care? What was the response and the reasoning? If turned down, what was the specific objection?

The company banned accounts involved in over five biological research cases, including grant drafting for gain-of-function experiments on the chikungunya virus and avian influenza mammalian-adaptation studies, while acknowledging it could not conclusively establish malicious intent behind every research effort. The findings highlight the operational challenge AI developers face in distinguishing legitimate scientific inquiry from work that provides capability uplift for hazardous operations. 1. What behavioral, account-level, and query indicators can distinguish potentially harmful dual-use biological assistance from legitimate academic research? 2. How effective are real-time safety classifiers at preventing multi-turn prompt engineering aimed at bypassing biological safeguards? 3. What governance framework should AI providers use to balance restricting high-consequence biological hazards against preserving model access for drug discovery and virology? 4. How do red-teaming methodologies evaluate whether a model provides actionable “capability uplift” in biological synthesis or gain-of-function protocols? 5. What role should verified institutional identity controls play as a prospective access model for biological research using high-capability models? 6. How can multi-provider threat-intelligence sharing be standardized while preserving user privacy and due process when accounts are suspended?

I am writing an upcoming feature for Medscape exploring the intricate feedback loop between mental health and obesity, specifically zooming in on the interoceptive facet. For decades, many individuals struggling with obesity have been conditioned by diet culture, chronic stress, or trauma to override their internal biological cues. This feature examines how clinicians are utilizing somatic therapy and interoceptive awareness training to help patients safely reconnect with their bodies, teaching them how to accurately translate physical sensations like hunger, fatigue, and emotional triggers. I am looking to speak with board-certified psychiatrists, psychologists, behavioral obesity medicine specialists, and licensed somatic therapists who clinicalize these techniques. Questions for Expert Respondents Please provide written responses (2-4 sentences per question) to the following five questions. Feel free to draw on clinical anecdotes (anonymized) or evidence-based practices. If you cite clinical studies in your answer, I'd really appreciate an accompanying link. The Override Mechanism: From a clinical perspective, how do chronic stress, trauma, and decades of restrictive diet culture structurally alter a patient's ability to perceive and trust basic internal biological signals (e.g., true hunger, early satiety, and fatigue)? Defining Interoceptive Training: How do you define and introduce interoceptive awareness training to patients who are deeply disconnected from or distrustful of their physical sensations? Somatic Integration: What specific somatic therapy techniques or exercises have you found most effective in helping patients differentiate between genuine physiological hunger and emotional triggers (such as anxiety, boredom, or shame)? Clinical Challenges: What are the biggest clinical hurdles or psychological safety barriers when patients begin to re-experience uncomfortable physical sensations, and how do you navigate them? The Obesity-Mental Health Loop: How does restoring interoceptive awareness practically interrupt or mitigate the broader feedback loop between mental health distress and metabolic/weight challenges in long-term treatment? Submission Guidelines Format: Please answer the questions directly in your response or paste a secure link. Credentials: Include your full name, clinical title, institutional affiliation, and a headshot/bio link if available. Please also provide a disclosure statement relative to the issues covered.

I'm looking for hospitalists and obesity medicine specialists to help with this story: Historically, hospitalists have viewed inpatient admissions as a strict "hands-off" zone for chronic lifestyle or weight-management drugs. Inpatient teams focus on stabilizing acute illness—treating decompensated heart failure, managing an acute kidney injury, or stabilizing glycemic crises—while reflexively deferring chronic preventative therapies back to outpatient providers. However, with obesity officially recognized as a chronic disease, waiting months for outpatient follow-up can mean a missed window for vulnerable patients with decompensated heart failure, severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), or poorly controlled metabolic disease. Recognizing the inpatient stay not just as a place of stabilization, but as a crucial care transition point, an emerging shift is taking root: initiating or re-optimizing weight-loss pharmacotherapy prior to discharge. I'd love it if you'd answer the below questions. When responding, please provide your complete title as you'd like it cited, your institutional affiliations, and please send along a disclosure statement relative to this topic. What clinical guardrails (renal function, volume, hemodynamics) must be met before starting anti-obesity medications in the hospital? How can hospitalists overcome the reflex to defer chronic disease management to outpatient providers during acute admissions? What specific workflows are needed to prevent medication reconciliation gaps or insurance hurdles between discharge and outpatient follow-up? How are inpatient teams navigating hospital formularies, bridging, and prior authorizations before patients leave? Which clinical criteria help identify patients who are appropriate for inpatient initiation versus those whose acute illness makes it unsafe? How is hospitalist training adapting to incorporate chronic disease prevention and obesity pharmacotherapy into routine rounds?

Hola Folks, we're writing a story on Trump's new potash deal with Belarus, and how it might cut Canada out of the picture. We're seeking agricultural economists, fertilizer-market analysts, commodity traders and supply-chain/logistics experts. Basically, Trump said on Sept. 21 that the U.S. is working on a major Belarusian potash deal at prices below Canadian supplies, but analysts note that Belarus’s landlocked geography and restricted access through Lithuania could make transportation considerably more complicated. USGS data also underscore how deeply the U.S. potash supply chain is tied to Canada. We need these queries answered for the story: 1. For readers unfamiliar with potash, what exactly is it, why is potassium so important to crop growth and yields, and why do American farmers use so much of it? 2. President Trump says Belarus could sell the U.S. potash for substantially less than Canada does. Once freight, insurance, port handling and other transportation expenses are included, could Belarusian potash actually be cheaper when it reaches an American farm? 3. Canada has an enormous geographic and infrastructure advantage in supplying U.S. farmers. What would the physical journey of Belarusian potash to the American Midwest look like, and where are the biggest logistical bottlenecks compared with moving Canadian potash south by rail? 4. With Belarus effectively cut off from its traditional Lithuanian export route, how dependent would a large U.S.-Belarus potash deal be on Russian railroads and ports? What additional transportation, sanctions, geopolitical or supply-disruption risks would that create for American buyers? 5. If the administration succeeds in bringing substantial quantities of Belarusian potash into the U.S., how might that affect fertilizer prices for farmers, Canadian producers and the broader North American potash market? Could simply introducing Belarus as a competing supplier put downward pressure on Canadian prices even if Belarus never replaces Canada as America's primary source? 6. USGS's analysis found that roughly 90% of U.S. net potash imports came from Canada in 2023, illustrating why replacing a meaningful portion of Canadian supply would involve much more than negotiating a lower mine-gate price. What's your take on that issue and why?

Hola Folks, we're writing a story on Trump's new potash deal with Belarus, and how it might cut Canada out of the picture. We're seeking agricultural economists, fertilizer-market analysts, commodity traders and supply-chain/logistics experts. Basically, Trump said on Sept. 21 that the U.S. is working on a major Belarusian potash deal at prices below Canadian supplies, but analysts note that Belarus’s landlocked geography and restricted access through Lithuania could make transportation considerably more complicated. USGS data also underscore how deeply the U.S. potash supply chain is tied to Canada. We need these queries answered for the story: 1. For readers unfamiliar with potash, what exactly is it, why is potassium so important to crop growth and yields, and why do American farmers use so much of it? 2. President Trump says Belarus could sell the U.S. potash for substantially less than Canada does. Once freight, insurance, port handling and other transportation expenses are included, could Belarusian potash actually be cheaper when it reaches an American farm? 3. Canada has an enormous geographic and infrastructure advantage in supplying U.S. farmers. What would the physical journey of Belarusian potash to the American Midwest look like, and where are the biggest logistical bottlenecks compared with moving Canadian potash south by rail? 4. With Belarus effectively cut off from its traditional Lithuanian export route, how dependent would a large U.S.-Belarus potash deal be on Russian railroads and ports? What additional transportation, sanctions, geopolitical or supply-disruption risks would that create for American buyers? 5. If the administration succeeds in bringing substantial quantities of Belarusian potash into the U.S., how might that affect fertilizer prices for farmers, Canadian producers and the broader North American potash market? Could simply introducing Belarus as a competing supplier put downward pressure on Canadian prices even if Belarus never replaces Canada as America's primary source? 6. USGS's analysis found that roughly 90% of U.S. net potash imports came from Canada in 2023, illustrating why replacing a meaningful portion of Canadian supply would involve much more than negotiating a lower mine-gate price. What's your take on that issue and why?

I'm writing a Blavity Health explainer on the GENEROUS Medicaid drug payment model. CMS announced Sept. 18 that all 50 states plus DC and Puerto Rico applied, with 40 states signed. My angle is the gap between the announcement and what enrollees actually experience, since KFF notes these models don't affect enrollee out-of-pocket costs, which federal law already caps at nominal amounts. Questions: 1. CMS framed this as bringing down drug costs for vulnerable Americans, but Medicaid copays are already capped at roughly $4 to $8. Who actually sees savings here, and how would an enrollee ever notice? 2. KFF says existing Medicaid rebates already cut gross drug spending by about 53%, which may limit what an international benchmark adds. How much room is really left? 3. CMS and manufacturers will negotiate uniform coverage criteria including prior authorization and step therapy. Could that change access for enrollees, for better or worse? 4. Work requirements and six-month renewals start January 2027. For someone on Medicaid right now, which matters more to their costs, this pricing model or those eligibility changes? 5. What's one thing you'd want a Medicaid enrollee to do in the next few months to protect their coverage? Please include your name, LinkedIn, credentials, title, institution, and any relevant financial relationships. Two to four sentences per answer is ideal, and I may quote directly.

Hola Folks, we're writing a story on Trump's new potash deal with Belarus, and how it might cut Canada out of the picture. We're seeking agricultural economists, fertilizer-market analysts, commodity traders and supply-chain/logistics experts. Basically, Trump said on Sept. 21 that the U.S. is working on a major Belarusian potash deal at prices below Canadian supplies, but analysts note that Belarus’s landlocked geography and restricted access through Lithuania could make transportation considerably more complicated. For readers unfamiliar with potash, what exactly is it, why is potassium so important to crop growth and yields, and why do American farmers use so much of it? 2. President Trump says Belarus could sell the U.S. potash for substantially less than Canada does. Once freight, insurance, port handling and other transportation expenses are included, could Belarusian potash actually be cheaper when it reaches an American farm? 3. Canada has an enormous geographic and infrastructure advantage in supplying U.S. farmers. What would the physical journey of Belarusian potash to the American Midwest look like, and where are the biggest logistical bottlenecks compared with moving Canadian potash south by rail? 4. With Belarus effectively cut off from its traditional Lithuanian export route, how dependent would a large U.S.-Belarus potash deal be on Russian railroads and ports? What additional transportation, sanctions, geopolitical or supply-disruption risks would that create for American buyers? 5. If the administration succeeds in bringing substantial quantities of Belarusian potash into the U.S., how might that affect fertilizer prices for farmers, Canadian producers and the broader North American potash market? Could simply introducing Belarus as a competing supplier put downward pressure on Canadian prices even if Belarus never replaces Canada as America's primary source? 6. USGS's analysis found that roughly 90% of U.S. net potash imports came from Canada in 2023, illustrating why replacing a meaningful portion of Canadian supply would involve much more than negotiating a lower mine-gate price. What's your take on that issue and why?
